title: The Gaussian Golem
intro: Everything from Week 1: distributions, Bayes, Gaussians, MLE, mixtures and gradient descent. It will hit you with multi-step problems like an exam would.

questions.scenario: **Scenario B (gradient descent).** Minimise $f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Ax-b^\top x$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&20\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(5,3)^\top$, start $x_0=(-3,-1)^\top$, so $\nabla f(x)=Ax-b$. Use step size $\gamma=0.05$.

questions.prompt: Part 2. Given a flag, what is $p(\text{fault}\mid\text{flag})$ (3 decimals)?

questions.prompt: *“To sample $\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)$ I draw $x\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and return $\Sigma x+\mu$.”* The bug is:
options: The covariance would be $\Sigma\Sigma^\top$; you need $L$ with $LL^\top=\Sigma$ (Cholesky)
questions.explanation: $\mathbb V[Lx+\mu]=LL^\top=\Sigma$ only when $L$ is the Cholesky factor.

questions.prompt: In EM for a Gaussian mixture, which is the correct order within one iteration?
options: Compute the expected probabilities $p(z)$, then update $\{\omega_k,\mu_k,\sigma_k^2\}$
Sample $z$ uniformly, then freeze the parameters
Both steps are done simultaneously by gradient descent only
questions.explanation: E (guess the hidden labels) then M (refit using the guesses).

questions.prompt: A student reports a higher *training* log-likelihood than a classmate and claims a better model. The correct response is:
options: Agree: higher training likelihood always wins
Compare on held-out data: generalisation (test performance) is the key factor
Agree, because the log-likelihood is the test metric
questions.explanation: Slide 20: generalisation capability, assessed on test data, is the key factor.
